claim: Zebrafish lacking Apelin signaling exhibit defects in endothelial tip cell morphology and sprouting.
source: Zebrafish lacking Apelin signaling exhibit defects in endothelial tip cell morphology and sprouting.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: In mosaic vessels, wild-type ECs leave the dorsal aorta (DA) and form new vessels while neighboring ECs defective in Apelin signaling remain in the DA.
source: Using transplantation experiments, we find that in mosaic vessels, wild-type ECs leave the dorsal aorta (DA) and form new vessels while neighboring ECs defective in Apelin signaling remain in the DA.
evidence: This claim is supported by transplantation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Apelin signaling enhances glycolytic activity in ECs at least in part by increasing levels of the growth-promoting transcription factor c-Myc.
source: Mechanistically, Apelin signaling enhances glycolytic activity in ECs at least in part by increasing levels of the growth-promoting transcription factor c-Myc.
evidence: This mechanistic claim is supported by metabolic assays and protein level measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: APELIN expression is regulated by Notch signaling in human ECs.
source: Moreover, APELIN expression is regulated by Notch signaling in human ECs, and its function is required for the hypersprouting phenotype in Delta-like 4 (Dll4) knockdown zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell culture experiments with Notch inhibition and activation in HUVECs.

claim: Apelin function is required for the hypersprouting phenotype in Delta-like 4 (Dll4) knockdown zebrafish embryos.
source: Moreover, APELIN expression is regulated by Notch signaling in human ECs, and its function is required for the hypersprouting phenotype in Delta-like 4 (Dll4) knockdown zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that loss of Apelin signaling blocks the dll4 morphant hypersprouting phenotype.

claim: Apelin (Apln) is a small secreted peptide, which was initially identified because of its inotropic activity.
source: Apelin (Apln) is a small secreted peptide, which was initially identified because of its inotropic activity (Szokodi et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Apelin was subsequently described as a tip cell-enriched gene.
source: Apelin was subsequently described as a tip cell-enriched gene (del Toro et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Apelin (Tatemoto et al., 1998), as well as the newly identified ligand Apela (Chng et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014), can both activate the Apelin receptor (Aplnr), a 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
source: Apelin (Tatemoto et al., 1998), as well as the newly identified ligand Apela (Chng et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014), can both activate the Apelin receptor (Aplnr), a 7-transmembrane G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mouse and frog embryos lacking Apln or Aplnr function exhibit reduced vascular outgrowth, decreased EC proliferation, smaller vessel diameter as well as defects in the alignment of arteries and veins.
source: Mouse and frog embryos lacking Apln or Aplnr function exhibit reduced vascular outgrowth, decreased EC proliferation, smaller vessel diameter as well as defects in the alignment of arteries and veins (Cox et al., 2006; Kälin et al., 2007; Kidoya et al., 2008; del Toro et al., 2010; Kidoya et al., 2010; Kidoya et al., 2015; Papangeli et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Apelin signaling has been implicated in several cardiovascular diseases including pulmonary hypertension, atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, and tumor angiogenesis.
source: In addition, Apelin signaling has been implicated in several cardiovascular diseases including pulmonary hypertension (Goetze et al., 2006; Alastalo et al., 2011; Chandra et al., 2011), atherosclerosis (Hashimoto et al., 2007; Chun et al., 2008; Kojima et al., 2010; Pitkin et al., 2010), myocardial infarction (Tempel et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017), and tumor angiogenesis (Kidoya et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2018; Uribesalgo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: apln, but not apela, expression was detected within the sprouting ISVs.
source: We detected clear alpn, but no apela, expression within the sprouting ISVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: aplnrb expression was detected in the ISVs.
source: For the receptor genes, we could only detect aplnrb expression in the ISVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: apln:EGFP expression was first detected in sprouting ISVs at 30 hpf.
source: We first detected weak apln:EGFP expression in sprouting ISVs at 30 hpf (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of the transgenic reporter line shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 54 hpf, all ECs within the dorsal longitudinal anastomotic vessel (DLAV) were labeled with apln:EGFP.
source: At 54 hpf, all ECs within the dorsal longitudinal anastomotic vessel (DLAV) – a vessel formed by tip cells – were labeled (Figure 1A, arrowheads) while some stalk cells also exhibited weak apln:GFP expression (Figure 1A, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of the transgenic reporter line shown in Figure 1A.

claim: aplnrb:Aplrnb-sfGFP expression at 26 hpf was visible in the entire ISV sprout but absent from non-angiogenic ECs within the dorsal aorta (DA).
source: Of note, aplnrb:Aplrnb-sfGFP expression at 26 hpf was visible in the entire ISV sprout (Figure 1B arrowheads), but it was absent from non-angiogenic ECs within the dorsal aorta (DA).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of the transgenic reporter line shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 54 hpf, aplnrb:Aplrnb-sfGFP expression was detected in all ECs that had sprouted out of the DA but also weakly in ECs within the DA.
source: At 54 hpf, aplnrb:Aplrnb-sfGFP expression was detected in all ECs that had sprouted out of the DA but also weakly in ECs within the DA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of the transgenic reporter line shown in Figure 1B.

claim: apln is expressed in tip cells while aplnrb is expressed in all sprouting ECs.
source: These results suggest that apln is expressed in tip cells while aplnrb is expressed in all sprouting ECs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression patterns observed in the transgenic reporter lines.

claim: apln -/-; apela -/- embryos exhibit a reduction in vascular sprouting at 28 and 54 hpf.
source: apln -/-; apela -/- as well as aplnra -/-; aplnrb -/- embryos exhibit a reduction in vascular sprouting at 28 and 54 hpf.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of mutant embryos shown in Figure 1C.

claim: aplnra -/-; aplnrb -/- embryos exhibit a reduction in vascular sprouting at 28 and 54 hpf.
source: apln -/-; apela -/- as well as aplnra -/-; aplnrb -/- embryos exhibit a reduction in vascular sprouting at 28 and 54 hpf.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging of mutant embryos shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Homozygous aplnra mutant embryos exhibited no obvious defects during ISV formation.
source: Homozygous aplnra mutant embryos exhibited no obvious defects during ISV formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Homozygous aplnrb mutant embryos exhibited reduced ISV length and failed to form the DLAV.
source: However, homozygous aplnrb mutant embryos exhibited reduced ISV length and failed to form the DLAV (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phenotype in aplnrb mutants was more severe in embryos lacking both aplnra and aplnrb, indicating partial compensation.
source: This phenotype was more severe in embryos lacking both aplnra and aplnrb (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating partial compensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis comparing single and double mutants shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Homozygous apela mutant embryos displayed only a mild delay in ISV outgrowth.
source: Homozygous apela mutant embryos displayed only a mild delay in ISV outgrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Homozygous apln mutant embryos exhibited defects in ISV outgrowth and failure to form the DLAV.
source: while homozygous apln mutant embryos exhibited defects in ISV outgrowth and failure to form the DLAV (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Loss of both apln and apela ligands increased the severity of the phenotype leading to ISV stalling at the horizontal myoseptum.
source: Loss of both ligands increased the severity of the phenotype leading to ISV stalling at the horizontal myoseptum (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic analysis of double mutants shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: No differences in sprout initiation or tip cell specification were observed in double homozygous receptor or ligand mutants.
source: However, no differences in sprout initiation or tip cell specification were observed in double homozygous receptor or ligand mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging and analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2A.

claim: Sprout elongation was slower in Apelin signaling-deficient mutant embryos, resulting in an overall reduction of sprout length.
source: Instead, we found that sprout elongation was slower in these mutant embryos, resulting in an overall reduction of sprout length (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2A and associated videos.

claim: Endothelial tip cells in wild-type embryos formed long filopodia which extended toward the dorsal side of the animal.
source: Furthermore, while endothelial tip cells in wild-type embryos formed long filopodia which extended toward the dorsal side of the animal (Figure 2A I, II, Figure 2—video 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2A and associated video.

claim: aplnr mutant embryos and aplnrb morphants displayed a blunted tip cell morphology.
source: aplnr mutant embryos (aplnra+/-; aplnrb -/- and aplnra -/-; aplnrb -/-) as well as aplnrb morpholino (MO) injected embryos (morphants) displayed a blunted tip cell morphology (Figure 2A III, 2A IV, 2B, C, Figure 2—video 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of mutant and morphant embryos shown in Figure 2A, 2B, 2C and associated video.

claim: aplnrb morphant embryos exhibit a reduction in the number of endothelial filopodia.
source: (C) aplnrb morphant embryos exhibit a reduction in the number of endothelial filopodia (Ctr MO, n = 10; aplnrb MO, n = 15).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of filopodia shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Apelin deficiency does not cause obvious defects in EC polarity.
source: Apelin deficiency does not cause obvious defects in EC polarity (aplnr +/+, n = 6; aplnr -/-, n = 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of Golgi apparatus location shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: aplnr mutants exhibited a reduction in ISV EC numbers of 1 cell at 30 hpf (4 instead of 5) and 2 cells at 52 hpf (5 instead of 7).
source: Compared to controls, aplnr mutants exhibited a reduction in ISV EC numbers of 1 cell at 30 hpf (4 instead of 5) and 2 cells at 52 hpf (5 instead of 7) (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of EC nuclei shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Global overexpression of apln did not lead to ectopic sprouting of blood vessels but led to mispatterned lymphatic vessels.
source: However, global overexpression of apln did not lead to ectopic sprouting of blood vessels but led to mispatterned lymphatic vessels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, arrows).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of heat-shocked transgenic embryos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Upon transplantation of wild-type donor cells into wild-type hosts, 34.5% of the donor-derived ECs were present in the ISVs at 24 hpf.
source: Upon transplantation of wild-type donor cells into wild-type hosts, 34,5% of the donor-derived ECs were present in the ISVs at 24 hpf (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of transplantation experiments shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Upon transplantation of wild-type donor cells into aplnr-deficient hosts, 80% of the donor-derived ECs were present in the ISVs at 24 hpf.
source: In contrast, upon transplantation of wild-type donor cells into aplnr-deficient hosts, 80% of the donor-derived ECs were present in the ISVs at 24 hpf (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of transplantation experiments shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The apelin receptors function cell-autonomously in endothelial sprouting.
source: Together these data show that the apelin receptors function cell-autonomously in endothelial sprouting.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the transplantation experiments showing differential behavior of wild-type vs. mutant ECs.

claim: ECs deficient for signaling though Gαi behave similarly to aplnr mutant ECs.
source: Our results show that ECs deficient for signaling though Gαi behave similarly to aplnr mutant ECs indicating that the Apelin receptor mediates its angiogenic effect through Gαi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pertussis toxin overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Apelin receptor mediates its angiogenic effect through Gαi.
source: Our results show that ECs deficient for signaling though Gαi behave similarly to aplnr mutant ECs indicating that the Apelin receptor mediates its angiogenic effect through Gαi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity between Gαi inhibition and aplnr mutation phenotypes.

claim: Wild-type donor-derived ECs in aplnr deficient embryos populated the entire dorsal part of the vasculature which is usually missing in these mutants.
source: Notably, wild-type donor-derived ECs in aplnr deficient embryos populated the entire dorsal part of the vasculature which is usually missing in these mutants, further confirming the cell-autonomous function of the Apelin receptors during angiogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of transplanted embryos at 54 hpf shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: dll4 morphants exhibited a hypersprouting ISV phenotype.
source: As previously reported (Leslie et al., 2007; Siekmann and Lawson, 2007), dll4 morphants exhibited a hypersprouting ISV phenotype (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of dll4 morphants shown in Figure 4A and citations to prior literature.

claim: A clear increase in apln:EGFP expression was observed in the ectopic sprouts of dll4 morphants.
source: Notably, we also observed a clear increase in apln:EGFP expression in the ectopic sprouts (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of dll4 morphants in the apln:EGFP reporter background shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The hypersprouting phenotype of dll4 morphants was not present when Apln or Aplnrb function was lost.
source: Strikingly, the hypersprouting phenotype of dll4 morphants was not present when Apln or Aplnrb function was lost (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of dll4 morphants in apln and aplnrb mutant backgrounds shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of aplnrb function in the background of the plxnd1 mutant did not alter its hypersprouting phenotype.
source: Loss of aplnrb function in the background of the plxnd1 mutant did not alter its hypersprouting phenotype (Figure 4C,E), suggesting that it is independent of Apelin function.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification of double mutants shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: Ectopic venous sprouting in response to bmp2b overexpression is independent of Apelin function.
source: Similar results were obtained when we analyzed ectopic venous sprouting in response to bmp2b overexpression (Wiley et al., 2011; Figure 4D,F).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that aplnr mutants still show ectopic sprouting in response to bmp2b overexpression.

claim: Apelin signaling is specifically required for Notch-modulated angiogenesis.
source: Together these data indicate that Apelin signaling is specifically required for Notch-modulated angiogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential requirement for Apelin in dll4 vs. plxnd1 and bmp2b hypersprouting phenotypes.

claim: An increase in APLN expression was observed upon Notch inhibition in HUVECs.
source: Consistent with the observations in zebrafish (Figure 4A), we observed an increase in APLN expression upon Notch inhibition (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis of HUVECs treated with DAPT shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Activating Notch signaling in HUVECs suppressed APLN expression.
source: Conversely to the Notch inhibition data, activating Notch signaling in HUVECs suppressed APLN expression (Figure 4H, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis of HUVECs stimulated with DLL4 shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The increased sprouting in response to Notch inhibition is, in part, driven by the upregulation of apln.
source: Together these data suggest that the increased sprouting in response to Notch inhibition is, in part, driven by the upregulation of apln.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations that Notch inhibition increases apln expression and that Apelin is required for the dll4 morphant hypersprouting phenotype.

claim: A marked reduction in glycolysis was observed after knockdown of Apelin signaling in HUVECs.
source: Notably, we observed a marked reduction in glycolysis after knockdown of Apelin signaling (Figure 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by ECAR measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mitochondrial oxygen consumption appeared unchanged after knockdown of Apelin signaling in HUVECs.
source: whereas mitochondrial oxygen consumption appeared unchanged (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by OCR measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A reduction in c-MYC protein levels was observed after depletion of Apelin signaling in HUVECs.
source: To gain insight into the underlying mechanisms, we analyzed key regulators of metabolism and found a reduction in c-MYC protein levels after depletion of Apelin signaling (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of PFKFB3 was reduced in Apelin signaling-deficient HUVECs.
source: Furthermore, expression of PFKFB3, which encodes an enzyme that sustains high glycolytic rates, was also reduced in Apelin signaling-deficient HUVECs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression of pfkfb3 in endothelial tip cells leads to a partial rescue of the vascular phenotype in aplnrb mutants.
source: In agreement with our in vitro data, we found that overexpression of pfkfb3 in endothelial tip cells leads to a partial rescue of the vascular phenotype in aplnrb mutants (Figure 5E arrowheads, 5F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mosaic rescue experiments shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: Apelin signaling controls the expression of regulators of glucose metabolism as well as glycolytic activity in developing endothelial cells.
source: Thus, Apelin signaling controls the expression of regulators of glucose metabolism as well as glycolytic activity in developing endothelial cells.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the metabolic findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Angiogenesis depends mostly on the function of the ligand Apln.
source: Here, we show that angiogenesis depends mostly on the function of the ligand Apln.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phenotypic analysis of apln and apela mutants showing stronger defects in apln mutants.

claim: Apela can partially compensate for the loss of Apln.
source: However, Apela can partially compensate for the loss of Apln.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that double mutants have more severe phenotypes than single mutants.

claim: Stage-specific ligand usage is in agreement with previous studies showing that apela expression is reduced by the end of vasculogenesis when apln starts to be expressed.
source: This stage-specific ligand usage is in agreement with previous studies showing that apela expression is reduced by the end of vasculogenesis when apln starts to be expressed (Chng et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on temporal expression patterns.

claim: The inhibition of filopodia formation by Latrunculin B treatment reduces ISV sprout length.
source: However, Phng et al., 2013 reported that the inhibition of filopodia formation by Latrunculin B treatment reduces ISV sprout length, suggesting that the ISV sprouting defects in apln mutants is caused by the filopodia defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The ISV sprouting defects in apln mutants is caused by the filopodia defects.
source: However, Phng et al., 2013 reported that the inhibition of filopodia formation by Latrunculin B treatment reduces ISV sprout length, suggesting that the ISV sprouting defects in apln mutants is caused by the filopodia defects.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity between Latrunculin B treatment effects and apln mutant phenotypes.

claim: Defects in EC numbers may also be contributing to the ISV sprouting defects in apln mutants.
source: However, one cannot exclude the possibility that defects in EC numbers are also contributing to the ISV sprouting defects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative explanations.

claim: Endogenous Apelin gradient might prevent ECs from ectopic sprouting in apln overexpression experiments.
source: However, these experiments were done in the presence of endogenous Apelin, and thus, it is possible that the endogenous Apelin gradient prevents ECs from ectopic sprouting.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of ectopic sprouting upon apln overexpression.

claim: Apelin might need to be expressed from a discrete source, rather than globally, to elicit a sprouting response.
source: In addition, Apelin might need to be expressed from a discrete source, rather than globally, to elicit a sprouting response.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of ectopic sprouting upon global apln overexpression.

claim: aplnrb is highly expressed in sprouting ECs in ISVs while being absent from non-angiogenic ECs in the DA.
source: Interestingly, aplnrb is highly expressed in sprouting ECs in ISVs while being absent from non-angiogenic ECs in the DA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the expression pattern observed in the aplnrb reporter line.

claim: ECs during tumor angiogenesis can be labeled by a CreERT2 transgene in the Aplnr locus while quiescent blood vessels in the surrounding tissue are not labeled.
source: These observations are in line with a recent study showing that ECs during tumor angiogenesis can be labeled by a CreERT2 transgene in the Aplnr locus while quiescent blood vessels in the surrounding tissue are not labeled (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Apelin signaling is a molecular switch to drive ECs into a pro-angiogenic state.
source: In addition to these signaling pathways, we propose Apelin signaling as a molecular switch to drive ECs into a pro-angiogenic state.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: aplnrb function regulates the ability of ECs to sprout or stay quiescent.
source: In line with the expression of aplnrb in sprouting but not quiescent ECs, we show that aplnrb function regulates the ability of ECs to sprout or stay quiescent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the transplantation experiments showing differential behavior of wild-type vs. aplnr mutant ECs.

claim: Notch signaling regulates the behavior of ECs.
source: Similarly, Notch signaling regulates the behavior of ECs (Siekmann and Lawson, 2007): rbpj deficient ECs contribute to the ISVs while wild-type ECs stay within the DA (Siekmann and Lawson, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Notch signaling regulates the expression of apln in vitro as well as in vivo.
source: Of note, we found that Notch signaling regulates the expression of apln in vitro as well as in vivo
evidence: This claim is supported by the HUVEC experiments and zebrafish dll4 morphant observations.

claim: Apelin signaling is a key downstream effector of Notch signaling during angiogenesis.
source: and that Apelin signaling is a key downstream effector of Notch signaling during angiogenesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genetic epistasis experiments showing that Apelin is required for the dll4 morphant phenotype.

claim: It is very unlikely that apln is a direct Notch target gene since activation of Notch signaling leads to a downregulation of APLN expression.
source: However, it is very unlikely that apln is a direct Notch target gene since activation of Notch signaling leads to a downregulation of APLN expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Notch activation suppresses APLN expression.

claim: PTEN has been shown to be required for Notch induced arrest in EC proliferation.
source: While PTEN has been shown to be required for Notch induced arrest in EC proliferation (Serra et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CXCR4 mediates Notch-controlled EC migration.
source: CXCR4 mediates Notch-controlled EC migration (Hasan et al., 2017; Pitulescu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PTEN and Apelin both regulate AKT phosphorylation.
source: PTEN and Apelin both regulate AKT phosphorylation (Davies et al., 1998; Masri et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AKT function might be a common effector of PTEN and Apelin signaling in EC proliferation.
source: Thus, one might speculate that AKT function is a common effector of PTEN and Apelin signaling in EC proliferation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the shared regulation of AKT by PTEN and Apelin.

claim: Apelin was required for EC migration in the absence of Notch signaling.
source: Furthermore, we found that Apelin was required for EC migration in the absence of Notch signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that Apelin is required for the dll4 morphant hypersprouting phenotype.

claim: CXCR4 is required for EC migration in the absence of Notch signaling.
source: Similarly, CXCR4 is required for EC migration in the absence of Notch signaling (Hasan et al., 2017; Pitulescu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CXCR4 and APLNR both signal through the G-protein Gαi.
source: CXCR4 and APLNR both signal through the G-protein Gαi (Moepps et al., 1997; Habata et al., 1999), and they might therefore have similar effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CXCR4 and APLNR might have similar effects due to their shared signaling through Gαi.
source: CXCR4 and APLNR both signal through the G-protein Gαi (Moepps et al., 1997; Habata et al., 1999), and they might therefore have similar effects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the shared signaling mechanism.

claim: Gpr124 has been reported to be required in tip cells during zebrafish angiogenesis.
source: Gpr124, another GPCR, has been reported to be required in tip cells during zebrafish angiogenesis (Vanhollebeke et al., 2015), similar to Aplnr.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Gpr124 is required in tip cells only in the brain.
source: However, Gpr124 is required in tip cells only in the brain (Vanhollebeke et al., 2015), while Aplnr is required in tip cells in the ISVs, where it is most highly expressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and contrasts with the broader expression of Aplnr.

claim: Apelin signaling regulates the expression of PFKFB3 and c-MYC, two powerful drivers of EC metabolism.
source: Here, we show that Apelin signaling regulates the expression of PFKFB3 and c-MYC, two powerful drivers of EC metabolism (Wilhelm et al., 2016; De Bock et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Western blot and RT-qPCR data showing reduced c-MYC and PFKFB3 levels upon Apelin knockdown.

claim: Apelin signaling promotes FOXO1 phosphorylation.
source: Recently it has been shown that Apelin signaling promotes FOXO1 phosphorylation (Hwangbo et al., 2017), which negatively regulates its activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXO1 has been shown to suppress c-MYC expression.
source: Consistent with these findings, FOXO1 has been shown to suppress c-MYC expression (Wilhelm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Apelin might signal through FOXO1 to regulate c-MYC levels.
source: Together these data raise the possibility that Apelin signals through FOXO1 to regulate c-MYC levels.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known relationships between Apelin, FOXO1, and c-MYC.

claim: Genetic deletion of Pfkfb3 in mouse ECs leads to a reduction in their number as well as defects in filopodia formation and extension.
source: Of note, genetic deletion of Pfkfb3 in mouse ECs leads to a reduction in their number as well as defects in filopodia formation and extension (De Bock et al., 2013b), phenocopying aplnr mutant embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genetic deletion of Pfkfb3 in mouse ECs phenocopies aplnr mutant embryos.
source: Of note, genetic deletion of Pfkfb3 in mouse ECs leads to a reduction in their number as well as defects in filopodia formation and extension (De Bock et al., 2013b), phenocopying aplnr mutant embryos.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity between Pfkfb3 deletion and aplnr mutant phenotypes.

claim: Manipulating the angiogenic state of ECs by controlling Apln signaling might have therapeutic potential to control vascular growth in pathological settings.
source: Taken together, our findings provide novel insights into a druggable pathway regulating angiogenesis and suggest that manipulating the angiogenic state of ECs by controlling Apln signaling might have therapeutic potential to control vascular growth in pathological settings.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the study's findings.

claim: ECs with higher levels of VEGF-A signaling become invasive tip cells that lead new vascular sprouts.
source: ECs with higher levels of VEGF-A signaling become invasive tip cells that lead new vascular sprouts, while neighboring ECs with lower VEGF-A signaling become trailing stalk cells (Gerhardt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Neighboring ECs with lower VEGF-A signaling become trailing stalk cells.
source: ECs with higher levels of VEGF-A signaling become invasive tip cells that lead new vascular sprouts, while neighboring ECs with lower VEGF-A signaling become trailing stalk cells (Gerhardt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Activation of Notch receptors by their ligand DLL4, expressed by tip cells, represses tip cell behavior in stalk cells.
source: Activation of Notch receptors by their ligand DLL4, expressed by tip cells, represses tip cell behavior in stalk cells (Hellström et al., 2007; Leslie et al., 2007; Siekmann and Lawson, 2007; Suchting et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of Notch signaling causes excessive tip cell formation and vascular overgrowth.
source: Loss of Notch signaling, on the other hand, causes excessive tip cell formation and vascular overgrowth (Hellström et al., 2007; Leslie et al., 2007; Siekmann and Lawson, 2007; Suchting et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: EC sprouting requires an increase in metabolic activity.

claim: Notch-deficient ECs outcompete wild-type ECs during ISV sprouting.
source: It has been previously reported that Notch-deficient ECs outcompete wild-type ECs during ISV sprouting (Siekmann and Lawson, 2007), an observation consistent with data in mouse (Jakobsson et al., 2010; Pitulescu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vascular sprouting and cell positioning within the sprout is tightly regulated by VEGF and Notch signaling.
source: At the molecular level, vascular sprouting and cell positioning within the sprout is tightly regulated by VEGF and Notch signaling (Hellström et al., 2007; Lobov et al., 2007; Siekmann and Lawson, 2007; Suchting et al., 2007; Jakobsson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PTEN and CXCR4 are downstream effectors of Notch signaling that control angiogenesis.
source: Thus far, two downstream effectors of Notch signaling have been reported to control angiogenesis namely PTEN (Serra et al., 2015) and CXCR4, another GPCR (Hasan et al., 2017; Pitulescu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vasculogenesis relies on the function of the ligand Apela.
